transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad you could make it in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. I appreciate it. It's, well, it's a bit of a long story, but I guess the main thing that brings me in today is that I just feel like I’m always moving from one thing to the next. I really just can’t seem to idle, you know? Like a car engine that's just constantly revving in neutral. 

I work as a customer service rep, and I've been doing that kind of work for a long time. Usually, I manage okay because I find ways to keep busy, but we recently had this whole overhaul at the office. They completely changed our floor plan, put us in these open pods where everyone can see everyone else, and they implemented this new strict scheduling system where you're glued to your headset. And, well, this new work setup has made my constant need to be doing something a lot harder to hide. 

It used to be that if the phones were quiet, I could get up, organize some files, pace around the breakroom, just kind of burn off that nervous energy. But now, I'm supposed to just sit there and wait for the next call, and I physically can't do it. I'm shifting in my chair, tapping my feet, bouncing from one browser tab to another, getting up when I'm not supposed to... My supervisor actually pulled me aside last week because it's becoming so obvious. I just can't sit still and do nothing, and it's really starting to put my job on the line.
Looking back, did you experience this same kind of restlessness or trouble sitting still when you were a child?

Well, yeah, actually. It's funny you ask that because, honestly, looking back, this whole... whatever you want to call it, this restlessness, it was around long before this recent job change. I mean, way back. If I really think about it, I can picture being in grade school, and it was always the same story. My mom kept a box of all my old report cards in the attic, and I remember looking through them a few years ago when we were clearing out her house. Every single year, it seemed like the teachers wrote the exact same thing. They'd always say I was a bright kid, you know, that I had potential and all that, but then there was always a "but." It was always, "He's bright, but he's careless," or "He rushes through things." 

And the talking—oh boy, the talking. They were always writing notes home about how I talked out of turn, how I couldn't just raise my hand and wait to be called on. It was like the thought would pop into my head and it just had to come out right that second, regardless of who else was talking. And staying at my desk? Forget about it. They constantly had to remind me to stay with my work, to sit down, to stop wandering over to the pencil sharpener or bothering the kid next to me. I just couldn't seem to just... be. So, yeah, this feeling of needing to be in motion, it’s not just the new office setup. It’s been trailing me around since I was in short pants, really. It’s just that now, at 57, you’d think I’d have figured out how to just sit in a chair, right? But it's like the older I get, the more that old grade school kid comes out when I'm forced to just sit there.
Outside of the physical restlessness, do you struggle to keep your focus on tasks that require sustained mental effort?

Yeah, I do. It’s... well, it’s frustrating, to be honest. I mean, take these coaching meetings we have to do now. They’re these long, drawn-out sessions where the supervisor goes over call metrics and quality assurance and all this new protocol stuff. And I go in there, you know, I sit down, I've got my notebook open, I've got my pen ready, and I tell myself, "Okay, pay attention, this is important." And for the first couple of minutes, I'm right there with them. I'm nodding, I'm tracking what they're saying. 

But then, it's like... I don't even know how it happens. It's like a switch flips in my brain, but without me touching it. Suddenly, I'll realize that the supervisor is still talking, their mouth is moving, but I haven't heard a single word they've said for the last five minutes. My mind is just... gone. I'm thinking about what I'm going to make for dinner, or remembering a movie I saw last week, or wondering why the ceiling tiles have that weird pattern. And it's the same thing when they hand out a new procedure manual or an update on the software we use. I'll start reading, and I'll get through a paragraph, maybe two, and then I'll realize my eyes are just scanning the words. They're moving across the page, line by line, but nothing is actually going in. I'm not absorbing any of it. I have to go back and re-read the same sentence three or four times just to figure out what it's supposed to mean, because my brain just refused to grab onto it the first time. It's incredibly draining, trying to force your brain to just stay on the track when it wants to go everywhere else.
Do you find yourself struggling with constant, uncontrollable worry about a variety of everyday matters?

No, not really. I mean, I wouldn't call it worry, you know? It's not like I'm sitting around chewing my fingernails about paying the electric bill or whether the car is going to break down or, I don't know, what the neighbors think of my lawn. I mean, sure, I have the normal stuff—everyone thinks about bills and work and all that—but it doesn't feel like a constant, uncontrollable dread or anything like that. It's more just... noise, I guess. 

Like, my brain is always busy, always buzzing, but it's not usually buzzing about bad things that might happen. It's buzzing about everything. Like I said before, it's the ceiling tiles, or a song I heard on the radio on the way to work, or wondering if I should try making chili this weekend instead of my usual spaghetti. It's just a constant stream of thoughts, a lot of jumping around, but it doesn't have that anxious, heavy feeling to it. I'm not lying awake at night terrified of the future, I'm lying awake at night because my brain decided it's the perfect time to remember every embarrassing thing I said in 1994, or to try and redesign my kitchen in my head. So, no, the worry isn't really the issue. It's just the sheer volume of thoughts, not so much what the thoughts are actually about, if that makes sense.
